synthesis:
The most “quality engineering” idea this week: stop pretending your data are independent just because you chopped them into windows. If you’re doing longitudinal ML (wearables, manufacturing sensor streams, repeated inspections), Alve et al. show you can get *spectacularly* wrong p-values—70–80% false rejections at a nominal 5%—unless your inference matches the unit you actually care about: the participant (or machine, line, lot).

### When correlated data masquerades as sample size

Alve et al. tackle a problem most of us have seen in the wild: you have 40 people (or 40 tools), but 40,000 windows. If you test at the window level, you’re essentially “counting the same subject 1000 times.” Their fix is refreshingly concrete:

1) Define a *participant-level estimand* (aggregate window predictions into one score per participant, then compute participant AUROC or similar).

2) For inference, run an *analysis-matched permutation test* that replays the entire label-dependent workflow under each permutation—folding, preprocessing, tuning, calibration, even pipeline selection if you did it.

That last bit matters. Leaving model selection outside the permutation null inflates Type I error fast (with 8 candidate pipelines, rejection jumps to 0.240 vs 0.040 when selection is properly rerun). Practically: if you’re shipping a “significant” model from a small cohort study, this paper is a checklist for what “honest inference” looks like.

### Auditing scoring reliability with an Ising model… powered by embeddings

Davier et al. do something I didn’t expect to work as cleanly as it does: they turn semantic similarity between constructed responses into *pairwise coupling* in an Ising model. Imagine each response’s score is a spin (0/1). Responses that are semantically close (cosine similarity of sentence embeddings) “want” to agree. Fit two parameters—temperature β and bias μ—using maximum pseudo-likelihood (so you avoid the nasty partition function), and you get:

- uncertainty quantification around scores,
- missing-label imputation,
- and a principled view of when a weighted-majority vote (their LiRA method) is actually approximating a coherent probabilistic model.

In simulation they hit accuracy 0.922 and κ 0.835 with only two fitted parameters, which is strong for a diagnostic layer. The practitioner catch: computing all pairwise similarities is \(K(K-1)/2\). They report scaling to ~6000 responses, but if you’re thinking “district-wide writing assessment,” you’ll want approximate neighbors or blocking.

### LLMs as causal-edge detectors: great recall, dangerous confidence

Kumar et al. deliver a needed cold shower for anyone tempted to use an LLM as a direct causal discovery oracle. Across models/prompts/graphs, edge predictions are overwhelmingly recall-dominant: precision suffers, graphs get dense, and false positives cluster where we most hate them—indirect paths and reversed directions. Worse, the model often sounds *very sure* while being wrong (80–100% verbal confidence on the majority of those false positives).

If you *must* use LLM judgments, agreement-based confidence (across prompts or models) behaves better than verbal or logit confidence for calibration and for throttling sparsity. The right mental model here is “soft prior that needs validation,” not “evidence.”

### DOE is having a moment in ML—and it’s not just hype

Two DOE-flavored pieces connect nicely:

- Mao et al. reframe LLM pretraining data mixing as a classical **mixture experiment**. Fit sparse second-order Scheffé surfaces, reveal interaction structure (web text complements lots of domains), and then design proxy runs with **model-robust I-optimal designs**. Net: recover mixture rankings with ~25% fewer proxy runs than Dirichlet sampling. If you’ve ever said “we’ll just sample a bunch of mixes,” this is the counterproposal: design it like we mean it.

- Eduku et al. make the equally practical point that surrogate choice should follow the **mathematical object**: MLPs for scalar responses, POD–SINDy for fields/dynamics. Even with only 5 CFD cases, they get meaningful spacing guidance (sweet spot near μ≈8) and quantify how much error is POD truncation vs SINDy rollout—exactly the kind of decomposition reliability engineers appreciate.

### Forward look

A theme ties the week together: *match the model—and the inference—to the unit and structure that generates the data.* Windows aren’t subjects. Similar texts aren’t independent labels. Proxy runs aren’t random draws if you can design them.

Question to chew on: where in our own workflows are we still “getting significance” or “getting agreement” mainly by accidentally multiplying correlated evidence?
